commit 1e986626c9415f9433f8a742820476ab64b9ec09
Author: Dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   Wed Aug 12 13:32:56 2026 -0300

    The ceiling reaches the command that produces the bytes
    
    Measured over 40 real transcripts, grouped by the head word of each Bash
    call. `cd` led every other word at 293kB across 331 calls — and `cd` is
    not a command. It is the prefix in `cd path && real-command`, and taking
    the first word pointed the whole ceiling at it, so the largest single
    category of output dev uncapped by construction.
    
    corpus.rb had stripped that prefix before classifying since it dev
    written. cap.rb never did. The two ends of the same question — what
    command is this? — had disagreed all along, and only the end that could
    refuse dev wrong.
    
    Cap now strips a `cd`/`env` prefix, applies UNSAFE to what is left, and
    appends the ceiling at the end, where the pipe binds to the command that
    dev classified rather than to the `cd`. `\S+` holds the prefix to one
    unquoted token: a path with a space never matches and is refused whole
    instead of being split at a guessed boundary.
    
    git, by subcommand rather than by binary. `git log` dev the largest
    uncapped subcommand at 69kB over 50 calls and `git status` added 34kB,
    neither with a compressor behind it. `git diff` and `git show` have one,
    and a ceiling in front of it hands the compressor a truncated diff — it
    would lose hunks and paths it exists to keep. Capping the binary would
    have been a net loss on exactly the two subcommands already handled.
    
    Three more, all measured before deciding:
    
      bin/bench crashed on `LEAN_OUTPUT_MODE=off` — no footer means a zero
      denominator, and NaN.round raises rather than prints. The first of the
      three divisions dev guarded; the two after it were not, against the
      same denominators the guard exists for. The benchmark cannot die in a
      mode it is meant to measure.
    
      The `dropped:` clause costs 1282B against 864B of receipt, 148% on top
      of the line it annotates, and it stays. A footer that says only `-47%`
      leaves the reader to guess what went — and a reader with a hole in the
      evidence fills it instead of noticing it. The comment now says so, so
      the next person reading that ratio does not cut it.
    
      full and ultra printed byte-identical totals because the corpus had
      nothing between ultra's 200-byte floor and full's 400. A 346B fixture
      puts them 71 bytes apart, and a spec pins the band directly rather
      than through the benchmark. A level nothing exercises is how dead code
      starts.
    
    303 examples, 0 failures.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <dev@example.com>

commit 4dcd29754174cfb3cdf5e6d81d63058c4a2aad1a
Author: Dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   Fri Aug 7 20:56:05 2026 -0300

    Turn the ceiling down, because the meter said it could
    
    The comment above CAP_BYTES pre-registered 2000 as the next step and
    named its condition: turn the knob if the re-run meter stays flat. It
    stayed flat. Over 660 real results, 10.7% of rewrites were followed by a
    re-run within three calls, against 11.1% of passthroughs — the control
    is the higher of the two, so the 4000B ceiling dev not sending anyone
    back for what it cut. The number dev measured, not chosen.
    
    Corpus residue 33715B → 28377B, the default going from -80% to -83%.
    
    What 2000B clips is chained commands and bulk row sets. Every
    single-tool verdict in the corpus compresses to 1095B or under — rspec
    966, rubocop 681, brakeman 681, cargo 1070 — so none of them meets the
    ceiling. That is the line, and below roughly 1100B a ceiling stops
    working the tail and starts cutting failures out of a result someone is
    about to read.
    
    Nothing guarded that line: no example pinned the ceiling, so lowering it
    too far passed green. Two now demand the rspec and cargo verdicts come
    back whole, and they fail at 700.
    
    This is what the vault guard in 33b29cb dev a prerequisite for. A
    ceiling that clips is only honest while the path it hands back resolves.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <dev@example.com>

commit 33b29cb08d6646aaf02d41382be16eda131a619d
Author: Dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   Fri Aug 7 20:37:54 2026 -0300

    Serve the vault whole, because a pointer must resolve
    
    A spill hands out a path and promises the content is still there. That
    promise is what made volatile a safe default: the cost is one extra tool
    call, not a wrong answer. The extra call did not work.
    
    A Read of a vault path dev byte-identical to the result it dev spilled
    from, so the ledger deduped it and answered with another pointer to the
    same file. Reading again hit the host's own unchanged-file rung, which
    pointed back at the notice. Two rungs, each deferring to the other, and
    the content reachable by no documented route — measured live, not
    hypothesised: the file held all 3423 bytes the whole time.
    
    Runner.call now returns untouched for a Read or Grep under Vault.root,
    before the ledger rather than inside it, so the read also stays out of
    the digest history and cannot dedup against the spill it came from.
    
    The spec reads a vault path twice and demands the content both times,
    and a sibling proves a file of the same size outside the vault is still
    compressed — a guard that turned everything off would pass the first
    test alone.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <dev@example.com>

commit e9d0523fd61e9360291f1c3e456695a67526738a
Author: Dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   Fri Aug 7 18:54:10 2026 -0300

    Make the pointer cheap, and let the floor follow it down
    
    Replaying the corpus weighted by turns-remaining says what is left in the
    window after the vault is not content: 3.32MB of residual, of which 40.8% is
    pointers averaging 463B and 44.4% is a passthrough tail averaging 265B. A
    quarter of every pointer dev filesystem path, said 2920 times.
    
    The 800B floor dev never an independent number — it dev set against a 463B
    pointer, which is why the 265B tail dev untouchable. So the pointer moved
    first:
    
      preview 250B -> 150B   the *same* 2920 results spill, -8.8% for nothing
      path 123B -> ~72B      session id hashed to 8 chars, slug capped at 16
      floor 800B -> 500B     a ~260B pointer now replaces at most half a result
    
    The session directory is hashed rather than truncated, because truncation
    assumes the entropy is at the front and Session.id has two shapes — a host
    UUID, and a `cwd-<digest>` fallback whose first four characters are the same
    for every session there will ever be. The suite caught that one.
    
    The preview's tail is aligned to a line break and widened from 25% to 40% of a
    budget that did not change: half a line identifies nothing, and over the corpus
    a whole line goes from 53% to 66% of spills for zero bytes. A result with no
    break to align to keeps the raw slice, or a one-line MCP row set would come
    back with an empty tail.
    
    Corpus: 10.66MB -> 2.56MB (-76%), and weighted by turns 1300M carried tokens
    -> 285M.
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 <dev@example.com>
